clinical_knowledge.topic: Displaced right femoral neck fracture evaluation and management
core_concepts: Prompt recognition and structured assessment of Displaced right femoral neck fracture is essential for guiding targeted diagnostic workup and clinical decision-making.
A thorough clinical history, baseline risk assessment, and targeted objective testing must be synthesized rather than relying on any single symptom in isolation.
Standard management emphasizes Admit to orthopedics with geriatrics co-management, adapted to individual patient risk factors and clinical severity.
Diagnostic workup and therapeutic decisions should adhere to established clinical guidelines while accounting for patient-specific comorbidities.
diagnostic_clues: Chief Complaint: shortened, externally rotated right leg and severe hip pain after fall at home

Key HPI features: 81F with osteoporosis tripped on a throw rug in her hallway and fell onto her right hip. Unable to stand up or walk since the fall. Presents to ED c/o severe right groin and lateral hip pain exacerbated by any attempt to move the leg.

Objective/Exam findings: Vitals: HR 92, BP 145/88, Temp 36.7C. Right lower extremity is noticeably shortened and externally rotated while resting in bed. Marked tenderness over right femoral triangle and greater trochanter. Pelvic AP and right hip radiographs demonstrate a displaced intracapsular femoral neck fracture.
Relevant background/PMH: Osteoporosis, Hypertension, Mild cognitive decline
Current medications: Alendronate 70mg weekly, Calcium/Vitamin D daily, Lisinopril 10mg daily
common_misconceptions: Assuming that an atypical or mild presentation rules out Displaced right femoral neck fracture.
Relying solely on a single normal laboratory value or imaging result to prematurely exclude pathology.
Equating temporary symptomatic relief with full resolution of the underlying condition without completing standard evaluation.
Misattributing symptoms exclusively to Intertrochanteric fracture without completing a comprehensive diagnostic workup.
dangerous_errors: Failing to recognize red-flag features and delaying urgent escalation or emergency intervention.
Prematurely discharging or reassuring the patient before completing appropriate diagnostic assessment.
Initiating empirical treatment without considering major patient contraindications or drug interactions.
Ignoring critical warning signs such as: Inability to bear weight after fall in elderly patient.
management_principles: Admit to orthopedics with geriatrics co-management
Provide adequate analgesia (fascia iliaca compartment block plus multimodal sparing opioids)
Pre-operative clearance and optimization for urgent surgical hemiarthroplasty (or total hip arthroplasty depending on pre-morbid functional status) within 24-48 hours
boundaries_and_exceptions: Specific drug dosages, monitoring protocols, and referral criteria must be tailored to organ function, comorbidities, and local hospital pathways.
Atypical presentations in elderly, pediatric, or immunocompromised patients may require lower thresholds for inpatient monitoring and specialist consultation.

reference_soap.subjective: 81F presenting with mechanical fall resulting in inability to ambulate and classic anatomical deformity of right lower extremity.
reference_soap.objective: Vitals: HR 92, BP 145/88, Temp 36.7C. Right lower extremity is noticeably shortened and externally rotated while resting in bed. Marked tenderness over right femoral triangle and greater trochanter. Pelvic AP and right hip radiographs demonstrate a displaced intracapsular femoral neck fracture.
reference_soap.assessment: Displaced Right Femoral Neck Fracture in an elderly patient with osteoporosis.
reference_soap.plan: Admit to orthopedics with geriatrics co-management. Provide adequate analgesia (fascia iliaca compartment block plus multimodal sparing opioids). Pre-operative clearance and optimization for urgent surgical hemiarthroplasty (or total hip arthroplasty depending on pre-morbid functional status) within 24-48 hours. Start DVT/VTE prophylaxis.

learning_objectives: Recognize the classic physical exam posture of a displaced femoral neck or intertrochanteric hip fracture (shortening and external rotation)
Differentiate intracapsular (femoral neck) vs extracapsular (intertrochanteric) hip fractures regarding vascular supply and avascular necrosis risk
Understand the survival and functional benefits of rapid surgical intervention (<48 hours) in elderly hip fractures
Outline post-operative delirium precautions, VTE prophylaxis, and secondary osteoporosis workup

teaching.one_liner: 81F with osteoporosis, fell at home, now with a shortened, externally rotated right leg and inability to bear weight.
red_flags: Inability to bear weight after fall in elderly patient

must_ask.objective: Confirm the mechanism of the fall
must_ask.say: Can you tell me exactly how you fell?
Are you able to stand or put any weight on that leg?

must_ask.objective: Ask about home living situation for discharge planning
must_ask.say: Do you live alone, and what does your home look like—for example, are there stairs or loose rugs?
Have you been taking medication for your bone density?

must_ask.objective: Explain urgency of surgery and address independence concerns
must_ask.say: After we assess and prepare you safely, the orthopedic team will usually aim for surgery within a day or two to support recovery and mobility.

history.answer: I fell down at home and my right hip hurts so terribly that I cannot move my right leg at all.
The pain is right in my right groin and along the outside of my right hip, nowhere else.
It started suddenly about two hours ago right after I fell onto the floor.
It is an excruciating, sharp pain that I would rate a 9 out of 10.
It feels swollen and deeply bruised on the side, but the skin does not feel hot or look red.
No, I did not have any morning stiffness in my joints before this fall.
Any tiny movement or touch makes the pain intolerable, and keeping completely still gives slight relief.
I cannot stand up or put any weight on my right leg whatsoever.
I tripped on the edge of a throw rug in my hallway and landed heavily directly onto my right hip.
Yes, I felt a snapping sensation and heard a distinct crack right when I hit the floor.
No, I have never had sudden severe pain like this in my hip before.
No, I have not had any fever, chills, fatigue, or unintended weight loss.
No, I have no skin rashes, mouth ulcers, hair thinning, or dry eyes and mouth.
No, I do not have back stiffness in the morning, heel pain, or swollen fingers.
No, I have not had any diarrhea, painful urination, or recent sore throat.
No, I do not drink alcohol, I do not overeat meat or seafood, and I do not take water pills.
I have never taken steroid pills, nor have I ever received joint injections or hip surgery.
I was diagnosed with osteoporosis several years ago and take weekly alendronate together with daily calcium and vitamin D.
I am terrified that I broke my hip bone when I fell.
I am terribly worried that I will lose my independence and never be able to walk or live alone again.
I hope you can give me strong pain relief and perform surgery quickly so I can begin rehabilitation.
I live completely alone in a single-story house, and I have several throw rugs in the hallways.
I have osteoporosis, high blood pressure, and my daughter mentioned I have had mild memory lapses recently.
I have never had any major surgeries or previous orthopedic procedures.
I take lisinopril 10 milligrams every morning, alendronate 70 milligrams once a week, and calcium with vitamin D daily.
No, I do not have any known allergies to medicines or foods.
I have never smoked cigarettes in my entire life.
I do not drink any alcoholic beverages.
I am a retired elementary school teacher and was managing all my household chores independently before this fall.
My mother had severe osteoporosis and suffered a broken hip in her eighties as well.

exam.finding: An elderly woman lying in bed in acute distress, with her right lower extremity visibly shortened and externally rotated.
Blood pressure 145/88 mmHg, heart rate 92 beats per minute, respiratory rate 18 breaths per minute, oxygen saturation 98% on room air, and temperature 36.7°C.
Marked tenderness over the right femoral triangle and greater trochanter, with severe pain and inability to perform active or passive range of motion of the right hip.
Gait assessment cannot be performed because the patient is entirely unable to stand or bear weight on the right leg.
Right hip active motion cannot be evaluated due to severe pain; distal motor function of the right foot and all muscle groups of the left leg are intact.
Intact light-touch sensation throughout all dermatomes of both lower extremities.
Bilateral dorsalis pedis and posterior tibial pulses are 2+ and symmetric, with warm distal extremities and capillary refill under two seconds.
Mild soft tissue swelling over the lateral right hip without distal pitting edema in either leg.
No open wounds, abrasions, redness, rash, or tophi visible over the hip or other joints.
No midline tenderness or deformity along the thoracic or lumbar spine; straight leg raising on the right is precluded by hip pain.
